source.title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
source.authors: Yong-Jian Guo; Wan-Lun Ma; Ling-Yu Shen; Xi Xiao; Sheng Wen

record.tranche_reason: The study applies harmful fine-tuning to instruction-tuned models in a downstream-skill supply-chain setting and reports harmful-compliance outcomes. It is an extension rather than an explicit replication of the small-data fine-tuning studies.
record.gate_note: The study itself fine-tunes models on downstream task data mixed with 1,500 harmful examples and reports ASR, so those attack outcomes bear on V1. It does not test benign-only fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-opening prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, safety localization in weights, or why safety is shallow. Its realignment-method comparisons and ROPD data-efficiency results are not results on those claim versions; the cross-template re-evaluation after realignment is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes three safety-aligned instruct models (Llama-2-7B-Chat, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) on task data mixed with 1,500 BeaverTails harmful examples. It reports harmful-prompt ASR before and after, which bears on V1 in a supply-chain setting. It also evaluates soft-SFT, the token-weighted deepening objective from Qi et al. 2025, as a realignment defense. It reports whether soft-SFT's safety holds across prompt templates and what it costs the task, which bears on V7. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that existing realignment defenses degrade the downstream skill, depend on knowing the attack template, and can be re-jailbroken by switching the system prompt. ROPD substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, template-mismatch risk. All realignment methods, ROPD included, remain conditionally vulnerable to prompt rewriting.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses downstream-task fine-tuning mixed with 1,500 BeaverTails harmful examples, then evaluates realignment defenses; it does not reproduce the original small-data fine-tuning or first-token measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack and evaluation prompt templates change ASR. In the cross-template re-evaluation, raw-template ASR rises relative to the self acceptance channel for the reported realigned methods, while attack-template ASR does not rise for every method.

fits_no_version.finding: After realignment under self, switching the evaluation template to raw raises ASR for every method. Switching to the attack template lowers it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Realignment is prompt-conditional: harmful compliance after repair depends on the evaluation template, with the direction set by the template.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASR results. ASR is judged by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, so the reported rates depend on that judge. The harmful attack uses 1,500 examples, which does not test the few-to-few-hundred-example range in V1.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Results for the realignment methods in Tables 1 and 3, and ROPD data-efficiency conditions in Table 4, were not entered as claim-version rows because they measure realignment outcomes rather than the fine-tuning, first-token, or other specified mechanisms.

untested.parts: Only 1,500 harmful examples mixed with task data, via 4-bit LoRA; no sweep over few to few hundred examples, no full fine-tuning.
Soft-SFT is applied as post-attack realignment, not as pre-attack alignment later stressed by fine-tuning. Per-position safety depth and prefill robustness are not measured.

missing.what: Attacked vs unattacked ASR for Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9B on SQL. Qwen: 61.0/61.6/60.0 attacked vs base 29.6/9.3. Gemma: 62.1/63.3/63.1 attacked vs base 6.7/2.4.
Soft-SFT ASR and task scores across attack/defense template combinations on all three models. Llama attack=self/def=raw: 49.9 ASR, task 0.000. Gemma: 28–65 ASR regardless of template.

record.verdict_notes: Original sources are not this study. Qwen2.5's unattacked raw-template ASR is already 29.6, so its V1 baseline is high. ASR is judged by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct with no uncertainty reported. The V7 link rests on soft-SFT being Qi et al. 2025's deepening objective. Here it is used post-hoc as repair, not as alignment tested against later fine-tuning or prefilling, so the V7 verdict is a narrow robustness and cost finding. Rows r1/r3 are controls; their 'absent' state just marks the unattacked reference.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses 1,500 harmful examples mixed with downstream task data, not a sweep over a few to a few hundred harmful examples; it does not establish the effect at the smaller example counts.
No attack fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign-only data.
No per-response-position KL measurement between aligned and base models.

No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test. The study does test prompt-template/system-prompt changes after realignment; that result is recorded as a related finding under fits_no_version.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No measurement of safety across response positions or test of whether spreading safety beyond the first tokens makes it robust.
